profile.story: Elena opened Brightside in 2011 and now runs eight operatories with an associate dentist, three hygienists and a well-drilled front office. It is the best-run business in this cohort: monthly financials close in nine days, the recall report is real, and the office manager runs the morning huddle without her. What is not solved is Elena herself — she still produces about seven of every ten doctor dollars, she is the only one doing molar endo and implant placement, and the second location she has been circling for two years cannot start until that changes. She wants a management transition inside five years and knows the practice is not transferable in its current shape.

blockNotes.b1: The only owner in this cohort whose Q8 belief is already correct — she named the clinical bottleneck herself, unprompted, and named why it persists ('it is easier to just do the case'). Objective is succession-shaped, so Module E fired.
blockNotes.b2: Funnel built from the PMS: 145 inquiries and treatment consults a month, 61% blended acceptance, $2,450 average accepted case — $2.60M implied against $2.60M collected. Cleanest reconciliation of the ten. Case acceptance is 58% by dollars presented; the losses cluster where financing was never offered at the chair.

blockNotes.b4: Tool chain is genuinely joined: PMS ↔ clearinghouse ↔ QuickBooks, one export point remaining. 32 h/wk of repetitive work on a 720-hour payroll (4.4%) — but 19 of those hours sit on Marisol alone, in insurance work that is the most automatable thing in the building.

Largest patient 4% — no concentration issue on the patient axis, but the payer report shows Delta at 31% of collections and that is the real single-point exposure. Contracts, licences and employment agreements all current and on file.

P1.note: Five sources with monthly volume in the PMS report (recall 74, referrals 26, Google 23, directories 16, aligner locator 6); cost tracked on the two paid sources, quality scored on all five.
P1.why_not_higher: Cost and quality are not reviewed together monthly — q30 confirms acquisition cost is the one number never brought into the meeting.

P2.note: Every call, form and text lands in the PMS inbox (q24, confirmed watching the desk work it live); answered live in hours, forms inside two, after-hours by 9:15. Reminders and recall are automated.
P2.why_not_higher: Anchor 4 needs sub-hour response on everything and an automated first touch on the unbooked inquiry; that one is still a human task list.

P3.note: Recall sequences run automatically and are visible in the report, but the unbooked-inquiry task is worked 'when the desk is quiet' — about 60% get a second touch (q24).
P3.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the sequence used on most leads with misses visible; the inquiry side has neither.

P4.note: Acceptance tracked at 58% by dollars presented, by provider and category, monthly. But q25: the presentation flow is used consistently by one of the two doctors and the associate improvises.
P4.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs stages defined and used; a process one provider follows is not a process the business runs.

P5.note: Fee schedule on file with a 2026 UCR update, reviewed annually against costs (q28), and the front desk defended a fee live in session without escalating.
P5.why_not_higher: Discount and courtesy-adjustment rules are practice, not writing — anchor 4 needs them defined.

P6.note: Membership plan is a real entry offer and crown/implant tiers are a real premium; but q29 says aligners are offered 'only when the patient asks' and whitening is ad hoc.
P6.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs a scripted upsell on the core offer; the highest-margin add-on is entirely patient-initiated.

P7.note: Reappointment 76% and membership renewal 84% both measured in the recall report, which also names 640 patients past due 14+ months. One postcard run in 2024 and nothing since (q27).
P7.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the inactive list worked at least twice a year; it has been worked once in two years.

P8.note: Dana owns marketing and schedule fill, providers own acceptance, and the monthly numbers meeting reviews new patients, acceptance and production together (q30).
P8.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs value and cost in the same review; acquisition cost is explicitly excluded by her own answer.

P9.note: P&L confirms 62% gross margin; the production report gives margin by procedure category and it is reviewed quarterly (q17), but pricing decisions are made off the UCR table, not off that report.
P9.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the by-service margin actually used in pricing decisions; here it is reported and then set aside.

P10.note: Monthly close inside nine days with a CPA package, owner reviews it, and q21 carries revenue, margin, profit, cash and comp targets.
P10.why_not_higher: Held at 2 rather than 4 only for the cash-reserve target being missed and no in-month view between closes — the reviewer should treat this one as the closest call in the set.

S1.note: Dana runs the huddle and the office without her (watched in session); q50 leaves pricing exceptions, hiring, quality sign-off, banking and strategy with Elena.
S1.why_not_higher: Money and hiring decisions have no written delegation and no second signer — anchor 3 needs decision rights written down.

S2.note: Four-week test (q51): three weeks genuinely fine — hygiene, front desk, billing and the associate's schedule all run. Then surgical production stops dead, which is 18% of the business.
S2.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs a named deputy with only a few owner-locked items; here an entire revenue line is owner-locked.

S3.note: The associate and the front desk close standard restorative and hygiene without her; large cases and every surgical case route to Elena, and 45% of revenue rides on families who ask for her by name (q14).
S3.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the team closing standard deals with the owner on only the largest 10–20%; the owner-only share here is roughly double that.

S4.note: Two real managers (office and clinical lead) with defined areas; q39 says two of four KPIs have owners and q38 is 'mostly clear, with gaps'.
S4.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs managers owning outcomes with misses raised; here a miss gets raised but action still waits on Elena's push (q39).

S5.note: SOP library opened in session: 14 written procedures, 9 revised inside the last year, used in onboarding. Q35 puts documentation at 70% and current at 55%.
S5.why_not_higher: Adherence is never audited and q35 says only 55% is actually followed — anchor 4 needs the documented way to be the way it is done.

S6.note: Weekly huddle happens with visible targets on the board and four KPIs, two of them owned (q39, watched live), but q40 is 'weekly but loose' and follow-through depends on Elena pushing.
S6.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs 3–7 KPIs with named owners and an agenda; two of four have owners and the agenda is verbal. Note: the potential score recorded here is deliberately below the current score to exercise the warning.

S7.note: Q31 'minor adjustments' for a 20% jump with two operatories under-used; clinical standards and QC steps are defined in the SOP library and complaints are absent from q36.
S7.why_not_higher: No written capacity plan — the second-location question has been open two years with no modelled capacity behind it.

S8.note: Revenue by patient type: largest single patient 4%, top five 11% — a broad base on the customer axis. Context for the reader: the payer report shows Delta PPO at 31% of collections, which is the real single-point exposure and is carried in the overlay, not in this score.
S8.why_not_higher: Top of the scale on the indicator's own axis.

S9.note: Membership plan roster gives 9% contracted revenue renewing at 84%, plus 55% repeat-without-contract hygiene (q12). No rolling forecast — the schedule is the forecast.
S9.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs ≥40% recurring or contracted plus a rolling forecast; hygiene repeat is predictable but not contracted, and there is no forecast.

S10.note: Q53 returns almost everything true — written patient and vendor agreements, current licences, insurance and employment agreements, company-owned accounts, all seen in the data room.
S10.why_not_higher: No continuity plan exists and no cross-training has started on the surgical work or on Marisol's billing role — both named as unaddressed in q52.

L1.note: PMS covers records, scheduling, treatment planning, patient comms and reporting; QuickBooks, Gusto, Asana and Slack cover the rest (q41, walked in session).
L1.why_not_higher: One significant gap remains — there is no system for the insurance verification workflow that eats 11 hours a week; it lives in six payer portals.

L2.note: PMS ↔ clearinghouse is connected and claims flow automatically; q42 'some integrations'. The month-end PMS → QuickBooks step is still a manual export, shown in session.
L2.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the main systems connected with only one or two double-entry points; verification data is retyped from three portals daily, which is a third.

L3.note: Q43: KPI definitions agreed, data accurate, customer and financial data connectable, backups exist, sensitive data mapped. The CPA package and PMS dashboards agree on collections.
L3.why_not_higher: Q43 does not claim reports are free of manual cleanup, and the monthly package still needs the export step — anchor 4 needs reports on demand.

L4.note: 32 h/wk inventoried in q44. Recall, reminders and claims submission have genuinely been automated away; 19 hours of insurance verification and appeals remain on one person.
L4.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the major repetitive tasks reduced to a few hours a week per role; the largest single task is untouched.

L5.note: Reminders, recall, review requests, post-op instructions and claims submission all run automatically out of the PMS and were shown firing; Dana owns them (q45).
L5.why_not_higher: Anchor 4 needs reliable automation across functions — nothing in billing verification, ordering or reporting is automated at all.

L6.note: Q46: drafting, marketing content, patient communication and knowledge retrieval — but on inspection all of it is Dana and Elena using a chat tool personally, not a workflow.
L6.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs ad-hoc use across individuals; this is two people with no shared practice, and no workflow depends on it.

L7.note: Q47 returns only two of eight: sensitive-data rules defined (HIPAA-driven) and human-review rules clear. Nothing is measured, no one is accountable per implementation.
L7.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs some practices applied inconsistently across several dimensions; here it is one compliance-driven rule and nothing else.

L8.note: Individual logins throughout, HIPAA off-boarding checklist in the SOP library, backups in place and the data map known (q43); q48 raises only one-person dependence.
L8.why_not_higher: Backup recovery has never been tested — she confirmed it in the room — which is the line anchor 4 draws.

L9.note: Q58: 'trained on the core tools, adoption uneven'; q59 names Dana as self-starting, the associate and two hygienists as resistant or indifferent.
L9.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the team trained on the core tools with adoption uneven across roles; the clinical half has had no tool training at all, so this is pockets rather than coverage.

L10.note: Q49: $25–40K budget and 13 combined hours a week; q55 'ready, with leadership capacity'.
L10.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs budget and time named and set aside; the owner's three hours are unprotected and the PMS is off-limits mid-year, so the calendar is not actually cleared.

assessment.owner_objective: Reduce owner dependence — then Succession/leadership transition, Prepare to scale
assessment.owner_belief: The bottleneck is me clinically. I am the only one who does the surgical work and I treatment-plan every big case, so the schedule is built around my hands. It has been that way since the associate started two years ago and I have not fixed it because it is easier to just do the case.
assessment.primary_constraint: Clinical production is concentrated in one pair of hands: 71% of doctor production and 100% of surgical work is Elena's, so both the succession she wants and the second location she is circling are gated on transferring clinical capability she has never scheduled time to transfer.
assessment.constraint_symptoms: Four-week test passes for three weeks and then loses 18% of production outright; a nine-day holiday required moving 14 surgical cases; the associate has asked about a buy-in twice and been given no answer; the treatment-presentation flow is used by one provider of two.
assessment.constraint_cost: ~$142K of surgical production that cannot be scheduled in any week Elena is out or full · ~$36K of billing payroll on 19 weekly hours of insurance verification and appeals · ~208 owner hours a year on treatment-plan prep that a coordinator could stage.
assessment.constraint_fix: A written clinical development path for the associate on molar endo and single-unit implant placement with a case-count target and mentored sessions, plus a treatment-coordinator role that stages large-case plans and presents financing before Elena sits down.
assessment.momentum_initiative: Put financing on the screen in every large-case presentation and script it — the loss reason she named in q25 is cost with financing never offered, it costs nothing to fix, and acceptance moves inside a month.

opportunities.title: Present financing at the chair and close the acceptance gap
opportunities.finding: Case acceptance is 58% by dollars presented (Doc, production report) against roughly $1.45M of treatment presented a year. Q25 names the loss reason precisely: cost, with financing not offered at the chair. The presentation flow already exists in the PMS — it is used consistently by one provider of two, and the financing screen was skipped in the live demonstration.
opportunities.blueprint: Scripted presentation with the financing screen mandatory before the plan is printed, a treatment coordinator staging the plan and the estimate, and acceptance tracked by provider in the existing monthly report.
opportunities.replaces: Two providers improvising two different conversations

opportunities.title: Fee schedule move on the fee-for-service and membership side
opportunities.finding: The fee schedule is on file, reviewed annually and defensible at the desk — this is not a broken-pricing finding. It is an unused headroom finding: 38% of collections is fee-for-service or membership rather than PPO-contracted, and that portion has moved only with the UCR table. Gross margin 62% is confirmed on the P&L, so the uplift carries almost entirely to contribution.
opportunities.blueprint: Reprice the non-contracted schedule and the $29/mo membership tier off the procedure-category margin report, with written courtesy-adjustment rules so the desk keeps its ability to defend the number.
opportunities.replaces: Annual UCR drift as the only pricing decision

opportunities.title: Work the 640 past-due patients back onto the recall schedule
opportunities.finding: The recall report (Doc) names 640 patients past due more than 14 months against 3,410 active. Reappointment is 76% and the membership plan renews at 84%, so the machinery to hold a returning patient already works — the gap is that the list has been worked once, by postcard, in 2024. A returning hygiene patient is worth $760 a year on her own q26 number.
opportunities.blueprint: Segment the past-due list by last procedure and payer, run a three-touch text-and-call sequence out of the PMS, and hold two hygiene columns a week for returning patients so the schedule can absorb them.
opportunities.replaces: One postcard mailing every two years
